source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 and GPT-4o beat Chinese students on the Remote Associates Test, a convergent task often used in incubation studies.
numbers: RAT, 61 humans, 30 items. Accuracy gap vs humans: GPT-3.5 +0.19, GPT-4 +0.26, GPT-4o +0.35 (all p<.001).
limits: Chinese-language materials; models may have seen items; no incubation delay was tested.
agent_relevance: Convergent association is not the bottleneck for LLMs. Do not add a step to fix it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Insight-task results were mixed by model: older models lost to humans on Chinese character puzzles and stumpers, GPT-4o beat humans; GPT-4-class models beat humans on rebus.
numbers: 60 humans. Character puzzle: humans above GPT-3.5 by 0.09 and GPT-4 by 0.09, below GPT-4o by 0.21. Stumper: humans above GPT-3.5 by 0.20 and GPT-4 by 0.06, below GPT-4o by 0.06 (p=.011). Rebus: humans below GPT-4-turbo by 0.32 and GPT-4o by 0.39.
limits: Accuracy only; training-data contamination is possible for puzzles.
agent_relevance: Insight-problem accuracy rose fast with model generation; a high score alone does not show an insight-like process.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: On a representational-change task (pick the restructured reading) humans clearly beat the models, even though models won on insight accuracy. Humans used transformation strategies; models used step-by-step reasoning.
numbers: Accuracy: humans higher than GPT-4-turbo by 0.46 (CI .41-.51) and GPT-4o by 0.31 (CI .25-.36). Strategy use: humans 72.41% transformation; GPT-4o 68.88% and GPT-4-turbo 71.26% reasoning.
limits: 61 participants; multiple-choice format; only two GPT models in this experiment.
agent_relevance: Suggests LLM insight scores can come from knowledge and inference, not restructuring. Restructuring may still need explicit scaffolding.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Models were more homogeneous and less novel than humans in creative writing, and their RAT answers stayed semantically closer to the stimulus.
numbers: Five-sentence story novelty: humans higher than GPT-3.5 (t=4.68), GPT-4 (t=4.75), GPT-4o (t=4.25), all p<.001. Homogeneity: humans lower, t from -9.14 to -16.65.
limits: Chinese sample; human raters.
agent_relevance: Weak support for an agent step that forces distant, diverse candidates before verification.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 era) solved verbal insight problems at about the typical human rate.
numbers: 30 problems (15 practice, 15 transfer); human solution rates from 20 subjects. ChatGPT total equalled the most probable human outcome and fell within the 5% most probable outcomes for practice and pooled sets.
limits: Small human sample (20); one model, early chat version; possible item leakage.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that insight-style puzzles were not out of reach for LLMs.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: A caution against anthropocentrism
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on a psychometric battery. Analytic problems failed completely; insight problems did better; repeated runs were unstable.
numbers: 5 insight problems. GPT-3.5 scored 1.5 to 3.5 of 5 over four runs; GPT-4 scored 4.5 of 5 on one run. Humans per item 44% to 61%. Analytic problems: 0 correct for both models. Item-level correlation with humans r=-0.63 (author says do not weight it, only 4 observations).
limits: Tiny sample; large run-to-run variance; partial credit for the non-insight route.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variance means one sample of an insight answer is unreliable; sample several.

source: Goldstein, Havin, Reichart & Goldstein (2023) Decoding Stumpers: LLMs vs Human Problem-Solvers
finding: Chat models beat humans at generating stumper answers but were worse than humans at checking answers. Verification, not generation, was the weak point.
numbers: 81 humans solved 38.15% (replicates 35% of Bar-Hillel 2021). GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 averaged 57.8% on the original set (43.4% on enhanced set); Davinci-2/3 29.6% (22.5%). Verification: humans 100% when they had generated the right answer and 63.8% when they had failed; models averaged 41%, below chance.
quote: humans exhibit superior skills in verifying solutions to the same problems
limits: Four models, one stumper set; prompt effect small and model-dependent (helped GPT-3, hurt chat models, interaction p=.005).
agent_relevance: Matches the schema stance: keep a separate verification step (the V of the four stages), because models do not check themselves well.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: On insight-like Japanese riddles, 38 LLMs scored far below humans; reasoning models did better than non-reasoning ones.
numbers: Human mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2, n=126, 120 items). Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. Full 201 items: odds ratio 2.29 (1.99-2.64) reasoning vs non; accuracy 9.42% vs 19.25%. GPT-5 inside the human CI (not formally tested). Release date correlated with accuracy, parameter count did not.
limits: Zero-shot, retrieval-free; Japanese wordplay; no formal model-by-model tests.
agent_relevance: Hard insight items were still unsolved by most models in 2025; the benchmark is renewable and usable as a test bed.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: Verification failure: models write the correct candidate in their thought log and then do not choose it. The generate-versus-endorse gap is the main failure.
numbers: Verification failures were 5% to 39% of a model's wrong answers across models with usable thought logs; a lower bound (verbatim match only).
limits: Only models with visible thought logs; strict string matching.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a guarded verification and stopping step after generation, rather than an incubation step.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo benchmark)
finding: Few-shot demonstrations that include reasoning raised accuracy in all four tested models; significant in two. The best model did not gain significantly. Thought-log language (English vs Japanese) had inconsistent effects.
numbers: Supplementary study, four models; gains not uniform and not shown across multiple demonstration sets.
limits: Small supplementary test; one demonstration set.
agent_relevance: Worked reasoning examples are a cheap scaffold lever; the effect is model-dependent.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Spontaneous mid-trace 'Aha' shifts in reasoning models are rare and usually go with lower accuracy.
numbers: 1M+ traces, Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Llama3.1-8B under GRPO; crosswords, math, Rush Hour. Shifts in 6.31% of traces overall; Qwen2.5-1.5B accuracy 2.57% with a shift vs 16.44% without. Formal Aha detector fires on 1.79% of samples. Shifts did not grow with training. Math average marginal effect -0.0615 (p=1.55e-4); Rush Hour about 0.
limits: Mostly small open models; GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 checked on math only (shifts 0.88-2.21% and 0.00-0.25%).
agent_relevance: The sudden-illumination story is not a reliable internal mechanism in LLMs; do not rely on it.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Externally triggered reconsideration helps when model uncertainty is high. A cue like 'Wait, something is not right, we need to reconsider' on a second pass lifted math accuracy.
numbers: Math Pass 2 accuracy 0.322 to 0.406, +8.41pp (entropy-gated, top 20% by sequence entropy); crosswords +0.45pp; Rush Hour +0.01pp.
limits: Gain tied to the entropy gate and to math; small or none elsewhere.
agent_relevance: A cheap uncertainty-gated 're-look' trigger is the machine analogue of ending an impasse. It worked in math only.

source: Kang et al. (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: Reflection after a first answer is mostly confirmatory and rarely changes the answer. Training with more reflection mainly lifts first-answer correctness.
numbers: Eight reasoning models, five math sets. Truncating reflection once a candidate appears cut reasoning tokens by 24.5% at under a 2.9% accuracy drop.
limits: Math datasets only.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking after a candidate exists is mostly waste; supports a stop rule over added reflection.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Understanding Aha Moments: from External Observations to Internal Mechanisms
finding: Studies 'aha moments' in reasoning models: more anthropomorphic self-reflection language and adaptive uncertainty on harder problems; claims it helps avoid 'Reasoning Collapse'.
numbers: Descriptive and latent-space analysis; I did not extract effect sizes.
limits: Conflicts with c11: their 'aha' is defined by linguistic markers, which c11 says track real strategy change poorly.
agent_relevance: Conflicting evidence on whether aha markers mean anything.

source: Lin, Snell et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: The closest working machine analogue of incubation: the model thinks about a context before the question arrives, then answers with less test-time compute.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; scaling sleep-time compute lifts accuracy by up to 13% (GSM) and 18% (AIME); 2.5x lower cost per query when one context serves many queries. o1 showed limited gains. Gain tracks how predictable the question is.
quote: by anticipating what queries users might ask and pre-computing useful quantities
limits: Needs a predictable future question; tasks were built to be stateful; no insight task.
agent_relevance: Offline pre-computation helps when the next question can be guessed. It is not incubation on an impasse, so the schema note (incubation not to add) stands.

source: Choi et al. (2026) IdleSpec: Exploiting Idle Time via Speculative Planning for LLM Agents
finding: Idle time while an agent waits for tools can be used to draft plans; IdleSpec beats vanilla and sleep-time compute on agent benchmarks.
numbers: GAIA+FRAMES average: Gemini-2.5-Flash 50.5 to 55.6 (+5.1); Gemma4-E4B 30.9 to 35.5; Qwen3.5-4B 33.2 to 40.0; MLE-Bench Any Medal up to +9.1%.
limits: Plans are guessed under observation uncertainty; three models.
agent_relevance: Closest agent-loop use of a break; it improves plans, not insight.

source: Choi et al. (2026) IdleSpec: Exploiting Idle Time via Speculative Planning for LLM Agents
finding: Sleep-time compute did not carry over to agent tasks: it gave no gain or hurt when the next observation is uncertain.
numbers: GAIA+FRAMES average, vanilla vs sleep-time compute: Gemma4-E4B 30.9 vs 31.0; Qwen3.5-4B 33.2 vs 29.4; Gemini-2.5-Flash 50.5 vs 50.1.
limits: Comparison run by the IdleSpec authors with their own baseline implementation.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a break only pays when the next input is predictable.

source: Helie, Sun & Xiong (2009) Mixed Effects of Distractor Tasks on Incubation (CogSci)
finding: Distractor effects on incubation are mixed. The CLARION model predicts that which module a distractor loads decides whether incubation is hurt. A human free-recall experiment found an incubation effect.
numbers: Cites Dodds et al. 2003: 29 of 39 experiments found an incubation effect. Experiment: 114 students, six groups of 19; condition effect F(5,108)=10.65, p<.001; Do Nothing above No Incubation (replicates Smith & Vela 1991).
limits: Free recall, not insight; distractor classes were model-derived.
agent_relevance: Model-based reason why incubation results conflict: incubation is several processes, not one.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (CLARION EII)
finding: A computational model of Wallas's four stages inside the CLARION architecture; incubation is implicit processing that continues while the explicit level is idle.
numbers: Press accounts (not the paper) report the coin problem solved 35.3% and 45.3% over 5,000 runs for two interruption conditions.
limits: Only press coverage seen; check numbers in the paper before use.
agent_relevance: Older AI system built on this subfield; a template for a hybrid explicit/implicit loop.

source: Nair, Gizzi & Sinapov (2024) Creative Problem Solving in Large Language and Vision Models: What Would it Take?
finding: Position paper with small tests. Maps Wallas stages onto ML: preparation to problem formulation, incubation and illumination to knowledge representation and manipulation, verification to evaluation. Cites the CLARION four-stage model and the Gizzi et al. 2022 framework.
numbers: Preliminary experiments on creative object substitution with four prompt classes (regular, affordance, task, task+affordance); I did not extract numbers.
limits: Position paper; no incubation delay tested.
agent_relevance: The usual machine mapping folds incubation into generic representation change, not a timed break.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: LLMs show an Einstellung-like fixation on red herrings in RAT-style groupings; removing red herrings raises scores sharply.
numbers: 494 walls; humans solved 285/494 walls and 1405/1976 groups. Best model GPT-4 10-shot connection F1 about 41-45% vs about 80% human. GPT models solved only single-digit walls on the original set; on OCW-WordNet (no red herrings) the same models solved several hundred.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; wall counts approximate.
agent_relevance: Fixation is real in LLMs, so the human story (fixation fades with time away) has a machine counterpart: reset context or re-sample.

source: Schapiro, Gladstone, Black & Ji (2026) Do Semantic Distance Tests Actually Predict Creativity in LLMs?
finding: The RAT, a staple of incubation research, mostly measures general model capability in LLMs, not creativity.
numbers: RAT validity vs creative writing benchmarks r=+0.62, +0.44, +0.51, but after controlling for general capability r|g in [+0.08,+0.28] (not significant); combinatorial creativity r=+0.58 falls to +0.14. 55 instruction-tuned LLMs. No test predicted output diversity.
limits: One paper (NeurIPS 2026); RAT scored by accuracy.
agent_relevance: Do not use RAT gains as evidence of creative gain in the agent.

source: Gwern (2025) LLM Daydreaming
finding: Proposal, not a test: a background day-dreaming loop where a generator links random concept pairs and a critic filters them. Cites incubation and sleep as human parallels.
numbers: No experiments. Author expects a low hit rate and calls the compute a daydreaming tax.
limits: Opinion essay.
agent_relevance: A concrete design for a machine incubation loop, untested.

source: Gap check (arXiv and web searches, Nov 2026)
finding: No controlled study found that varies an incubation delay or distractor for an LLM and compares it to human incubation.
numbers: arXiv search 'incubation language model creativity' returned 0 results; web searches returned only the papers above.
limits: Absence in my searches only; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, so coverage may be incomplete.
agent_relevance: The incubation effect itself has not been tested in LLMs; the schema should not assume it transfers.

source: Raz et al. (2024), as cited in Zhang et al. (2025)
finding: Cited as finding that GPT-4 significantly outperformed humans on verbal insight tasks.
numbers: No numbers seen; second-hand.
limits: Primary paper not found in my searches; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Orru 2023 and Goldstein 2023.

source: Gizzi et al. (2022), as cited in Nair et al. (2024)
finding: A creative problem solving framework for ML inspired by the four stages.
numbers: No numbers seen; second-hand.
limits: Primary paper not opened.
agent_relevance: An older AI scaffold built on the stage model.

source: Dream-COP (2026), arXiv 2610.36618, listing only
finding: Replays past search trajectories to guide LLM discovery of combinatorial optimization algorithms, a replay-style offline step.
numbers: No numbers; saw only a one-line summary.
limits: Not read; the link to sleep consolidation is my inference.
agent_relevance: Possible agent-loop use of offline replay; check before citing.
